extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and scratchwork explaining proof strategies (direct proof, contrapositive, cases, factoring, epsilon-delta, limits) for elementary number theory and analysis exercises. Emphasizes how to translate assumptions into algebraic forms and choose efficient proof methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct conditional proof (assume hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional statement, assume the hypothesis is true and show the conclusion follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: assume parity/divisibility hypotheses (e.g., n | a, n | b or n = 2k) and manipulate to express the conclusion in the required form (e.g., ax+by = n(kx+ℓy)). The text repeatedly uses 'assume the hypothesis and show the conclusion' as the primary approach for direct proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions concretely (parity and divisibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate qualitative statements into their definitions: write even as 2k, odd as 2k+1, n|a as a = nk, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer applying definitions and prior results rather than heuristic chains (e.g., write numbers in forms 2k or 2k+1; avoid informal multiplicative reasoning without justification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reusing bound-variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: When expressing multiple integers in defined forms, do not reuse the same dummy variable (e.g., don't use k for both m and n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep separate integer parameters (k, ℓ, m, ...) to avoid confusion in algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show divisibility by factoring common divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n|a and n|b, write a = nk and b = nℓ and factor to show n divides linear combinations like ax+by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: ax + by = nkx + nℓy = n(kx+ℓy); then identify integer m = kx+ℓy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic manipulations of equalities to exhibit divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply and subtract equalities obtained from divisibility assumptions to produce desired multiples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from a = 2k and a = 3m, multiply and subtract to get a = 6(k−m), proving 6|a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with heuristic multiplicative chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't rely on informal reasoning like 'if 2|a and 3|a then 6|a' without working through definitions, because analogous reasoning can fail for other numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always prefer formal manipulations using definitions (counterexample: statement about divisibility by 4 and 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive as strategy when direct proof is hard
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a conditional as its contrapositive to place the assumption on the simpler term and simplify the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving parity or modular statements is often easier via contrapositive; convert 'if complex expression then simple property' into 'if not simple property then not complex expression' and handle cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases for 'or' hypotheses or weak assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When hypotheses are 'or' statements or give little structure, split into cases that exhaust possibilities (e.g., parity cases, residues mod n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: n even/odd, remainders upon division by 3/5; sometimes many nested cases occur—try to minimize by clever choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'without loss of generality' (WLOG) carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When two cases are symmetric, prove one and invoke WLOG to avoid repetition, but first check the cases are truly similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always convince yourself by sketching both possibilities; misuse of WLOG can introduce subtle errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional proofs require two implications
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'iff' statements, prove each direction separately: (A⇒B) and (B⇒A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates splitting biconditionals into two conditionals and proving them in turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples to test converses
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether a converse statement holds, find explicit numerical counterexamples if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: converse 'n|ab ⇒ n|a or n|b' is false; take n=4, a=b=2 to disprove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make exponents comparable to multiply roots
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving closure properties for integer roots with different exponents, raise to common power (e.g., akℓ and bℓk) so bases can be multiplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows using kℓ to obtain (ab)^{kℓ} = nℓ m^k and conclude integer root property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't apply non-monotone functions to inequalities without checking monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If x < y, you cannot assume f(x) < f(y) unless f is known to be increasing on the interval of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the function is increasing on the domain before applying it (example: square-root is increasing on [0,∞]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization tricks (difference of squares, product of consecutive terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use algebraic factorizations to simplify expressions and reveal divisibility or sign structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a^2−b^2=(a−b)(a+b) to relate sqrt inequalities; factor (n^2−1)(n^2+2n)=(n−1)(n+1)n(n+2) to reason about divisibility by 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse-scratchwork for inequalities involving roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Start from the desired inequality, manipulate to a clearly true statement, then reverse the steps in the formal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove √(x+y) ≤ √x + √y, begin with assumption as scratchwork then reverse logic in write-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient partitioning of cases for absolute values
rubrics_metrics.description: When handling absolute values, partition the real line only at sign-change points of the expressions to minimize cases (e.g., x<−4, −4≤x≤3, x>3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessarily splitting into overlapping or nested cases; choose minimal intervals where signs are constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality as a bounding tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Use |a+b| ≤ |a| + |b| to derive bounds and to 'add zero in a fancy way' to introduce convenient terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bounding |x+1| via |(x−1)+2| ≤ |x−1|+2; derive |x+1| < 3 when |x−1|<1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding products by bounding factors (ε-δ technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: When |(x−1)(x+1)| appears, bound one factor by restricting δ (e.g., force |x−1|≤1 so |x+1|≤3), then choose δ=min{1,ε/3}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose auxiliary constraints on δ to control 'other' factors; combine constraints using min.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor and bound in epsilon-N and limit proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor target expressions to separate terms with known smallness (e.g., 1/n^2 and 1/n^3), then compare and bound the smaller term by the larger to simplify inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show 2/n^2 + 3/n^3 < ε by noting 1/n^3 ≤ 1/n^2 for n≥1, so bound by 5/n^2 and choose n large enough (n > sqrt(5/ε)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose concrete δ or N from algebraic inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate desired error bounds into explicit formulas for δ or N (e.g., δ≤ε/3, δ=ε/3, N>1/√ε, N≥M^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work algebraically to isolate the variable and then pick a convenient choice satisfying all constraints (often via min or max).

rubrics_metrics.name: Squeeze/sandwich reasoning for limits involving bounded functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bounds like |sin θ| ≤ 1 to dominate complicated terms and reduce to simple inequalities on x or n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bound |(6x sin(1/x))|/|x| ≤ |6x| and then force |6x|<ε by choosing |x|<ε/6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation formulation for showing non-convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a sequence does not converge to L, exhibit ε>0 such that for all N there exists n>N with |a_n−L|≥ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subsequence behavior (e.g., oscillation) to pick ε and show persistent distance from any candidate limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use finite maxima to bound initial terms when proving boundedness from convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining a uniform bound for tail terms (choose ε=1 to get |a_n|<|L|+1 for n≥N), take the maximum of finitely many initial |a_i| to obtain a global bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct M = max{M0, |L|+1} where M0 bounds the first N−1 terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler reorganizations to avoid messy algebra (strategic inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with several terms, compare sizes and bound the whole expression by a single dominant term to simplify (e.g., bound 2/n^2 + 3/n^3 by 5/n^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for monotonic relationships (1/n^3 ≤ 1/n^2) to reduce complexity and avoid unnecessary square roots or convoluted algebra.
